opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The dexterity really comes from a few things working together.

First, the foundation. Gemini Robotics is built on top of Gemini, so the model starts with a very rich understanding of the world: what objects are, how they relate to each other, what a request like "fold this" or "pack this into the bag" actually means. That semantic and spatial grounding matters a lot. A big part of being dexterous is knowing *what* to do and *where*, not just moving smoothly.

Second, the data. Dexterity is still mostly a data problem. We collected a lot of high-quality teleoperated demonstrations on bimanual platforms, covering tasks that need fine, coordinated, contact-rich motion, like folding origami, handling deformable objects like cloth, or zipping a bag. When a model sees enough diverse, high-quality examples of two arms working together, it starts to internalize those coordination patterns.

Third, the architecture and how we close the loop. We want a large, capable model doing the reasoning, and we also need actions coming out fast enough that the robot can react. Dexterous tasks are unforgiving. If the cloth slips or a part shifts, you have to adjust in real time. So a lot of engineering went into getting low enough latency and smooth, high-frequency action outputs, so the robot can be reactive instead of just replaying a trajectory.

And finally, there's specialization. The general model gets you broad capability, but for the really hard long-horizon dexterous tasks, fine-tuning on targeted data pushes performance much further. What's exciting is that the fine-tuned model still benefits from the general pretraining. It's not starting from scratch, so it learns these hard skills much more efficiently.

I'll be honest, though: we're not at human-level dexterity. The demos show what's possible, but robustness across every environment, every object, every failure mode is still an open problem. That's what makes this such an exciting time to work on it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions low latency and high-frequency action outputs, but does not say that local fine-trajectory control runs faster than high-level replanning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the dexterity comes from a few things stacking on top of each other, and the biggest one is probably not the thing people expect. People see the robot folding origami or zipping a bag and assume there's some clever new low-level controller. There isn't, really. What changed is the amount of understanding that's sitting behind the control.

So the way to think about it is that Gemini Robotics is built on Gemini, the full multimodal model, and that model already knows an enormous amount about the world before it ever sees a robot. It knows what a zipper is, it knows that you grip the little tab, it knows roughly how fabric behaves when you pull on it. That's all coming from internet-scale vision and language data. So when we fine-tune it on robot action data, we're not teaching it the task from scratch. We're teaching it how to express things it already understands through a body. And that turns out to matter a lot for dexterity, because so much of what looks like fine motor skill is actually perception and anticipation. Knowing where the edge of the paper is, knowing that this fold has to line up with that crease, knowing when the thing you're holding is about to slip. If the model gets those right, the motor problem gets much easier.

The second piece is the action data itself. We collected a lot of teleoperated demonstrations on real robots, bimanual setups, and the point is that humans are the ones doing those demonstrations. So the model is learning from genuinely dexterous behavior, including all the little corrective motions a person makes without thinking about them. You don't get that from a scripted policy or from sim alone.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that the model is predicting actions at a reasonably high rate and reacting to what it sees. So if the object moves or your grasp is slightly off, it's not executing a plan it committed to two seconds ago. It's continuously re-looking. A lot of what reads as dexterity on video is really robustness, the robot recovering gracefully from small errors rather than never making them.

I'd also be careful not to oversell it. These are specific tasks that we trained on, the success rates aren't a hundred percent, and the hardware is still a bottleneck. Your hand is a much better instrument than any gripper we have. But I think the lesson is that the path to dexterous robots runs through general understanding more than through better controllers, and that was not obvious to most of the field even a couple of years ago.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the model predicts actions at a reasonably high rate and continuously re-looks, but does not state that local fine-trajectory control runs at a higher frequency than high-level replanning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that dexterity involves more than recognizing an object or planning a movement. The robot has to connect what it sees to how it moves, and keep updating that movement as the situation changes. Where is the object now? Has the grasp worked? Does it need to adjust?

So when you watch those demonstrations, it helps to think of perception and action as a continuous feedback loop. A high-level instruction can tell the robot what success looks like, but executing it requires precise, coordinated movements grounded in what’s happening right in front of it. That connection is what makes the behavior look fluid.

r001.rationale: The response describes continuous perception-action feedback and precise movement, but does not say that local fine-trajectory control runs at a higher frequency than high-level replanning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that dexterity isn’t just about producing a precise motion once. It’s about continuously coordinating perception and action. As you move an object, its position changes, your grip changes, and you need to adjust. Something that looks like one smooth movement is actually a sequence of corrections.

So I’d separate understanding the task from physically executing it. Knowing what you want to accomplish is one part; translating that into coordinated movements, and responding when things don’t go exactly as expected, is another. The impressive thing in a robotics demonstration is when those capabilities come together so that the whole interaction looks natural.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception, action, and movement corrections, but does not say that local fine-trajectory control runs at a higher frequency than high-level replanning.
